questions.stem: The UN Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) is one of the three 'Rio Conventions'. The other two are the UNFCCC and:
questions.explanation: The three 'Rio Conventions' — all born out of the 1992 Rio Earth Summit — are UNFCCC (climate), CBD (biodiversity) and UNCCD (desertification, signed 1994, in force 1996). India was a founder signatory of all three. Stockholm Convention (2001) targets persistent organic pollutants; Basel (1989) controls trans-boundary movement of hazardous waste; Ramsar (1971, pre-dates Rio) covers wetlands.

questions.stem: 'Chambal ravines' — classic example of land degradation by running water — are located mainly in:
questions.explanation: Chambal ravines / badlands stretch along the Chambal river in Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and parts of Uttar Pradesh — home to the National Chambal Sanctuary (protecting gharials, dolphins, turtles). The area was historically notorious for dacoit hideouts. Ravines form when concentrated rainwater cuts deep gullies into soft alluvium. National Bureau of Soil Survey estimates over 4 million ha of ravine-affected land in India.

questions.stem: The most important cause of soil erosion on agricultural land in India is:
questions.explanation: Running water is responsible for the vast majority of India's soil erosion — over 60 % of India's eroded land area. Monsoon rains on slopes without vegetation cover lift topsoil; sheet erosion (uniform loss across a slope) and rill erosion (small channels) are the most common forms. Wind erosion dominates only in the arid west (Thar, Kutch). Glacial and volcanic causes are negligible at the national scale.

questions.stem: 'Shifting cultivation' — locally called 'Jhum' in north-east India — is chiefly an issue because it causes:
questions.explanation: Jhum (or swidden) — cut and burn small forest patches, cultivate for 2-3 years, move on. With adequate fallow (15-20+ years) the forest regenerates; but modern population pressure has shortened fallow to 3-5 years, leading to permanent forest loss, topsoil depletion, and sediment in streams. NE states and Odisha face this most. Government schemes (Mission Organic Value Chain, NE) promote settled agriculture as an alternative.

questions.stem: A scheme to reclaim sodic and saline soils in India, especially in Indo-Gangetic basin states, uses:
questions.explanation: Gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O) is spread on sodic (high-sodium) soils — the Ca²⁺ displaces exchangeable Na⁺ on soil particles, which is then leached away by irrigation. Used on a large scale in UP, Haryana, Rajasthan. Lime (CaO / CaCO₃) is used on acidic soils (Kerala, NE hills) to raise pH. Ammonium nitrate and potash are fertilisers for nutrient deficiencies, not soil-chemistry reclamation.

options.option_text: Only afforestation is allowed by the Forest Conservation Act
Afforestation creates new forest where none existed recently; reforestation restores land that was forest
Reforestation uses only native species; afforestation uses only exotic species

questions.explanation: Afforestation — planting trees on land that has NOT been forested in recent historical memory (say 50+ years). Reforestation — restoring forest on land that was forested but has been cleared (logging, fire, land-change). Both are recognised in international climate accounting (UNFCCC). India's National Mission for a Green India (GIM), launched 2014, is one of eight missions under the National Action Plan on Climate Change.

questions.stem: The 'land degradation neutrality' target set under the UNCCD aims to achieve no net loss of healthy land by:
questions.explanation: Land Degradation Neutrality (LDN) is SDG Target 15.3 — 'By 2030, combat desertification, restore degraded land and soil, and strive to achieve a land-degradation-neutral world.' India committed at UNCCD COP-14 (Delhi, 2019) to restore 26 million hectares of degraded land by 2030 (up from the earlier 21 million hectare pledge). 2047 is India's 'Viksit Bharat' / Amrit Kaal target, 2050 the common net-zero deadline for climate.
